blocks.text: Least-to-most prompting breaks a complex problem into a sequence of simpler subproblems, ordered from easiest to hardest, then solves them one at a time, feeding each answer forward as context for solving the next, harder subproblem.

This topic covers how the decomposition and sequential solving stages work together, how this differs from plan and solve prompting covered earlier in this module, and why solving the easiest subproblem first tends to make the hardest, final subproblem noticeably easier to get right.
1. What Least-to-Most Prompting Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473223610-747680203.png

Least-to-most prompting has two distinct stages, first decomposing a complex problem into an ordered sequence of subproblems, simplest first, then solving each subproblem in that order, using the answer from each prior subproblem as context for solving the next.
2. Decomposing Into an Ordered Sequence of Subproblems

blocks.alt: Decomposing Into an Ordered Sequence of Subproblems
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473223610-829153524.png

The decomposition step identifies a natural progression, a version of the problem that is genuinely simpler, a version slightly more complex than that, and so on, until the final subproblem in the sequence is effectively the original full problem.

code.content:
prompt_decompose = (
    "Break this problem into a sequence of simpler subproblems, "
    "ordered from easiest to hardest, ending with the original problem itself."
)

blocks.text: 3. Solving Subproblems in Sequence
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473223610-927358332.png
After decomposition, each subproblem gets solved in order, and the answer to each one is explicitly carried forward as additional context when solving the next, harder subproblem in the sequence.
4. The Two Stage Process, in Practice

blocks.alt: The Two Stage Process, in Practice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473223611-506174293.png

In practice this typically involves at least two model calls, one to produce the decomposition itself, and then one additional call per subproblem in the sequence to actually solve it, using all previously solved subproblem answers as accumulated context.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Stage","What Happens"],"rows":[["Decomposition","The full problem is broken into an ordered subproblem sequence"],["Sequential solving","Each subproblem is solved using all prior answers as context"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Least-to-Most vs Plan and Solve
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473224486-844575966.png

Plan and solve prompting, covered in an earlier topic, writes a full plan and then executes all of it, typically within one continuous pass, least-to-most is more explicitly sequential, each subproblem answer becomes concrete, carried forward context for the next call, rather than all steps happening within a single reasoning pass.
6. Why Solving the Easiest Subproblem First Helps

blocks.alt: Why Solving the Easiest Subproblem First Helps
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473224488-908027255.png

By the time the model reaches the hardest subproblem, which is effectively the original full problem, it already has correctly solved answers to every simpler version building up to it, this accumulated, verified context tends to make the final, hardest step noticeably more reliable than attempting the full problem cold.

blocks.title: This is particularly useful for problems that scale in difficulty
blocks.content: Least-to-most was specifically designed for problems where a model handles easier versions well but struggles with harder versions requiring the same underlying reasoning applied more times or at greater complexity.

blocks.text: 7. Least-to-Most vs Chain of Thought

Chain of thought, covered in an earlier topic, reasons through one continuous chain within a single pass, least-to-most explicitly restructures the problem into separate subproblems solved across multiple calls, with genuine intermediate answers rather than just intermediate reasoning steps carried forward.
8. The Cost, Multiple Sequential Calls

Like self-consistency and tree of thoughts, both covered earlier in this module, least-to-most requires more than one model call, at minimum one for decomposition plus one per subproblem, this cost needs to be weighed against the reliability improvement for problems that genuinely benefit from it.
9. When Least-to-Most Is Worth It
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473224488-896006803.png

Least-to-most earns its extra cost specifically for problems that are genuinely compound, built from a progression of increasingly complex versions of the same underlying task, for a simple, single step problem, the decomposition and sequential solving overhead provides little real benefit.
Worked Example

A developer building a math tutoring assistant finds that a model solves simple two step arithmetic word problems reliably, but struggles with a five step version of the same underlying problem type, occasionally dropping a step.

Applying least-to-most, first decomposing the five step problem into a sequence from a one step version up to the full five step version, then solving each in order and carrying forward each correct answer, the model successfully solves the full five step version, since by that final step it already has four correctly solved intermediate answers to build on rather than needing to track everything in one continuous attempt.
Common Mistakes

items: Applying least-to-most to a simple, single step problem where the decomposition overhead adds no real benefit
Not carrying forward the actual solved answers from earlier subproblems as context for later ones
Confusing least-to-most with plan and solve, which executes a full plan in one pass rather than sequential calls
Decomposing a problem into subproblems that do not actually build toward the original problem in increasing difficulty

blocks.text: Practice

Take a problem that scales in difficulty, a word problem with an easy two step version and a harder five step version, decompose the harder version into a sequence from simplest to full problem, and solve each subproblem in order, carrying forward each answer, then compare this to solving the full problem in one attempt.
Key Takeaway

Least-to-most prompting decomposes a complex problem into an ordered sequence of subproblems, from simplest to the original full problem, then solves them one at a time, carrying forward each correct answer as context, making the hardest, final step noticeably more reliable for problems that scale in difficulty.
